When Aikozho in his motley robe
Stood between us—
He was the spiritual patron I revered—
And solemnized our marriage for the Last Judgment,
Khan Saikal, daughter of Karacha Khan,
Made this promise:
‘When you die, for forty days
I shall attend your funeral rites,’ she said,
And swore upon the Quran.
Send word to Khan Saikal;
When Saikal comes, bury me.
On that day, my fierce one,
You may do as you please.
In the land called Lower Crimea,
Forty days' journey away,
Lives Urumkan's son Kokboru.
Together we stirred clouds in the sky
And pledged friendship into the next world.
We joined when tiny as lice,
United when small as thumbs;
Together we played and wrestled.
In the city of Lower Mecca
We studied for five years.
We talked together,
Pledging friendship thrice in one day.
Send word to Kokboru;
Let my poor soul not depart with eyes unclosed.
Ever acting as befits his name,
Let your greathearted one's honor suffer no loss through this.
Listen, hapless Kanykei, I have something to say.
There are forty holy men in Andijan:
Have them brought here
To perform my rite of absolution.
Let Andijan's Aikozho
Attend my funeral prayer.
Be sure to bring him;
Spend my livestock,
Giving him half of all I own!
The reason you must give it:
When drunk on mare's milk,
I imprisoned Aikozho
And beat the forty holy men.
When they truly angered me,
I plundered their turbans
And penned them up like dogs.
When drunk on liquor,
When young and lacking sense,
I persisted in drinking grain beer
And beat him till he wailed.
I took liquor and drank it.
When I go to the next world,
Kanykei, what shall I do about
The transgression laid upon my neck?”
So Manas muttered,
His thin mustache lying flat,
As though bound for Judgment Day.
Manas turned and lay upon his side,
His keen eyes peering faintly.
Khan Manas was in a dreadful state,
As though bound for Judgment Day,
Seized by distress, his limbs gone slack.
Seeing this sickness of his,
His thin mustache lying flat,
As though bound for Judgment Day,
She saw his eyes rolling wildly,
As though bound for the next world,
Gravely ill, his limbs gone slack.
Coughing with crack upon crack,
Exhausting his fierce wife,
He lifted his head from the pillow.
When he rose and cried, “Oh!”
Blood poured out in gushes.
Wailing and weeping without cease,
Kanykei lost her strength.
Coughing with thud upon thud,
He lifted his head from the bed.
When he rose and cried, “Oh!”
From the sovereign's mouth
Blood poured out by the bowlful.
Weeping in anguish and crying out,
Your sister-in-law lost her strength.
As the blue-maned khan grew sicker,
Unable to twist her reinlike hair,
Your sister-in-law could not stand for shrieking and weeping.
Your sovereign fell dreadfully ill.
The dark blood issuing from his mouth
Filled twelve whole pits.
Seeing the blood that flowed,
Your sister-in-law screamed and wept,
Unable to find even a fly's worth of help:
“The leopard's hour of death has come;
This black-faced woman has no recourse.
My brow bone slopes away;
When my sovereign has passed away,
This black-faced woman's fortune will be scant.
This poor head will drink mare's milk no more.
When the lord has passed away,
I shall yearn even for brackish water.
When the mighty one's eyes close,
My poor life will be abased.”
Then Manas said these words
(His illness now beyond all measure):
“Kanykei, its collar gold, its sleeves brass,
Its double mail with lark's-eye links,
Its brocade sash, its ample jacket,
Reinforced in places with fine iron wire,
Thwarting even Kelte's bullets,
Beyond the reach of arrows,
Impenetrable to steel points,
Though one fought six months without rest,
No bullet could pierce it.
I had Andijan and Kokand searched;
The cotton of the Six Cities and Kokand
I had brought in as tribute.
I had every part made strong,
Had it worked without stint.
Wearing it satisfied the heart;
No howling blizzard touched the body.
Akolpok, fit for battle—
Kanykei, lay it over me!
Let me turn my face to the True One;
When the angel of death draws near,
Let me close my eyes saying, ‘Allah!’
Until my dear soul gives its cry,
With Akolpok, worn in firefights,
Let me comfort myself.
Slung over the back, a mirror to the moonlike shoulders,
When life is sorely pressed,
A solace to the soul held in trust,
A matchlock when fired in play,
A Koichagyr gun when striking in earnest,
The living gun Akkelte—
Earlier, beyond Andijan,
On this side of Namangan,
Under the khan of Kokand's wing,
From the moon-yellow plain,
Sixty Russian land surveyors,
When they came forth,
When I turned my steed toward them,
When we stood opposed,
Fled away in a clattering rush.
Those sixty Russian champions,
Slaughtered and plundered in the field—
Akkelte, taken as booty,
Kanykey, lay it beside me!
Let me repent before Allah;
Until my appointed due draws near,
Let me take comfort in it.
When the angel firmly lays on his five hands,
Only then shall I let it be.
Until my entrusted life departs,
Until my death comes directly,
The living musket Akkelte,
Lay it beside me;
Let me take comfort in that.
The gray leather belt descended from heaven,
The belt that befriends dear life,
When I myself reached eleven,
‘Bind this about your waist,’
Father Aykojo said as he gave it.
The face of the earth stirred;
Every living soul stood still.
Aykojo, who gave the belt,
Vanished unseen from sight.
When I entered a desperate battle,
When I shouted and bound it at my waist,
The forty hidden saints became my companions.
When I saw a hostile foe,
When I girded it in fury,
A black-spotted leopard
Raged beside my flank.
When I shouted and bound it at my waist,
A short-tailed lion
Prepared at my side.
The gray leather belt descended from heaven,
The belt that befriends my life—
Those who knew told the tale:
It came from the unseen,
Found through God's love.
‘A belt descended from heaven,’ they said.
The ignorant, who did not know, said:
‘When he oppressed Kokand,
When he conquered Marghilan,
He imprisoned the dervish,
He beat the wandering holy man.
Driving white deer as cattle,
Throwing the earth into uproar,
Then he seized the belt by force.’
So spoke the ignorant, who did not know.
Kanykey, hang it close beside me!
The great Quran brought from Mecca,
My lady, place it beneath my head!
The six keen blades descended from heaven,
The very finest swords:
Zulpuqor, which Manas received;
Achbolot, which Ajybai received;
Kylbolot, which Bakai received;
Zhoykuma, which Almambet received;
Achalbars, which Chubak received;
Arkesken, which Syrgak received.
Those were the six keen steels,
When their anger was provoked,
Those treasures that shattered the world.
When drawn from the sheath with a shout,
They never went idle without drinking blood.
When eagerly taken from the sheath,
Without drinking blood they never returned to it.
Hearing their fame,
The enemy fled in dread.
Never turning back from stone,
Never drawing back from iron,
The six sacred keen blades,
Kanykey, lay them beside my head!
That Syrnayza, taken for jousting,
When raised in darkness,
Flashed as though the moon shone.
When thrust at a hostile foe,
Twisted and drawn, it flashed.
If a fly alighted, it rang;
If a whip-handle touched it, it clanged.
Its point was fashioned without a join:
‘Wherever it strikes,
May the wounds worsen till death,’ they said,
And tempered it with human tears.
When I saw a confronting foe,
When we came face to face,
I gripped it for the thrust.
However great the strain,
That wretch would never break;
It bent like a cauldron's circular stand.
Among the Russians on the right,
Syrnayza brought devastation.
Among the Chinese on the flank,
Syrnayza brought slaughter.
Prop it close beside me!
Kanykey, let me turn toward the Truth;
When my appointed due draws near,
Then shall I close my eyes.
Now while I am alive,
Taking the lance for my support,
Let me take comfort in it!
If by chance I die,
Kanykey, if you die with me,
If we both die,
And Semetey is left behind,
Let him not ride a gray bullock when migrating.
Abyke and Köbösh, the six scoundrels,
Must not keep him always as a shepherd.
Let them not send him after cattle,
Beat the only son while young,
And make him cower;
Abyke and Köbösh, the six scoundrels,
Must not take revenge like this!
Kanykey, cross the Küyük pass and go!
Scatter your many possessions and go.
